description: The Toro 21-inch Super Recycler is the best gas lawn mower for most yards because its cast aluminum deck cannot rust. Five more push and self-propelled picks.
dek: The Toro 21-inch Super Recycler is the best gas lawn mower for most yards because its cast aluminum deck cannot rust.
intro: The best gas lawn mower for most buyers is the Toro 21-Inch Super Recycler Personal Pace, because its cast aluminum deck cannot rust and its drive matches your walking speed. On a flat lawn under about a quarter acre, a simple push mower such as the Craftsman M115 or Troy-Bilt TB110 does the job for far less.

Gas is no longer the automatic choice for every yard. It earns its place on larger lawns, in thick or often-overgrown grass, and for anyone who wants to finish on one tank instead of watching a battery gauge. If that sounds like your lawn, you have three choices left to make: whether you need a drive, what the deck is made of, and whether you will spend roughly twenty minutes a season on engine care. This guide ranks six gas mowers and answers the questions owners ask most, from engine size to why a mower will not start.
quickAnswer: Buy the Toro Super Recycler if you want one gas mower to last a decade, the Toro Recycler 22-Inch for most of that ease at a mid price, and the Troy-Bilt TB230 for budget self-propulsion on flat ground. For small level lawns, the Craftsman M115 and Troy-Bilt TB110 are the best gas push mowers on a budget, and the Cub Cadet SC 100 leaves a cleaner cut.

blocks.p: Three of the six are self-propelled and three are push mowers. Pick the type first by lawn size and slope, then choose within it. Past half an acre, look at a rider or a [zero turn mower](/best-zero-turn-mower/) instead of any walk-behind.

sections.h: The 6 Best Gas Lawn Mowers in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: The ranking weighs manufacturer specifications (drive system, deck material, engine and warranty), parts and service availability, and the patterns that repeat in owner feedback. These mowers were not put through hands-on trials for this guide; each write-up notes when a claim comes from a spec sheet or from owners.

blocks.h3: Best Overall: Toro 21-Inch Super Recycler Personal Pace

blocks.p: The Super Recycler is the gas mower to buy if you plan to keep it for the long haul. Its deck is cast aluminum rather than stamped steel, so it cannot rust through at the seams the way neglected steel decks eventually do, and owners commonly keep these mowers running long after cheaper machines are scrapped. The recycler deck shape keeps clippings circulating so they are cut several times before falling, leaving fine mulch that disappears into the turf. The Personal Pace handle reads the pressure of your hands and sets ground speed to match, so there is nothing to adjust. You pay a clear premium over steel-deck competitors and carry extra weight compared with a plain push mower, so skip it if your lawn is small, flat and your budget is tight. On a quarter to half acre with an owner who keeps tools for years, the deck alone justifies it.
**Pros:** Rust-proof cast aluminum deck; Personal Pace drive; excellent mulching; broad Toro network. **Cons:** Higher price than steel-deck mowers; heavier than push mowers.

blocks.h3: Best Mid-Price Self-Propelled: Toro Recycler 22-Inch Personal Pace

blocks.p: The standard Recycler gives you Toro's Personal Pace drive and a well-shaped mulching deck at a price close to mainstream self-propelled mowers. Its 22-inch deck is an inch wider than the usual 21, which trims a few passes off a typical suburban lawn. Owners commonly call the drive intuitive: lean in and it speeds up, ease off and it slows. The deck is steel, so scraping it clean and storing it dry matters for rust resistance, and the front-wheel drive loses grip on steep slopes or when the bag is full. Up to roughly half an acre of level or gently rolling grass, few gas mowers are less hassle, and the handle folds down for storage. Choose the Super Recycler for the lifetime deck; choose this one if saving money comes first.
**Pros:** Personal Pace drive at a mid price; 22-inch deck; good mulching; folds for storage. **Cons:** Steel deck needs cleaning; front drive weaker uphill.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Toro+Recycler+22+inch+Personal+Pace&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Budget Self-Propelled: Troy-Bilt TB230

blocks.p: The TB230 is a plain self-propelled gas mower priced below most rivals with a powered drive. Power goes to the front wheels at one set pace, which works well for an even-paced walker on flat ground. Its tall back wheels roll over uneven spots without gouging the turf, and the 3-in-1 deck switches between bagging, mulching and side discharge. Owner reviews say it starts reliably as long as the gas is fresh and routine service is kept up. Expect thinner components than on premium machines, and scrape the steel deck often or rust will creep in. One fixed speed can feel too quick for some walkers and too slow for others, so try it in a store if you can. For a flat lawn up to about a third of an acre, it is the best gas value lawn mower with a drive.
**Pros:** Low price for self-propelled; high rear wheels; 3-in-1 deck; easy parts. **Cons:** Single speed; lighter build than premium mowers.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Troy-Bilt+TB230&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Budget Push: Craftsman M115 21-Inch

blocks.p: The M115 is a gas push mower and nothing more, which is exactly its appeal. For about as little as any big-name gas mower costs, it gives you a 21-inch steel deck, a common small engine and all three clipping modes. Leaving out the transmission keeps the weight and the parts count down, a good trade on compact level lawns that are easy to push. Owners treat it as a dependable first mower, provided it gets fresh gas and a new plug and air filter every season or two. The limits are obvious: pushing gets tiring on bigger lawns and any slope, and the handle and wheels are basic. Under about a quarter acre of level grass, it is all the gas mower you need.
**Pros:** Very low price; 3-in-1 deck; light and simple; widely stocked parts. **Cons:** No drive; basic handle and wheels.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Craftsman+M115&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Value Push: Troy-Bilt TB110 21-Inch

blocks.p: Troy-Bilt's entry push mower stands out for its larger rear wheels, which roll over bumpy turf more easily and make pushing a little less tiring on lawns that are not perfectly smooth. The 21-inch deck bags, mulches and side-discharges, and the design is simple enough that most owners handle routine service themselves. Owners commonly praise its reliability with basic care. Its limits are the usual push-mower ones: keep it to small level lawns, and do not park the steel deck wet and caked with grass. Choosing between this and the Craftsman M115 usually comes down to price and what your nearest store stocks; the TB110 gets the nod for uneven turf. A spare blade and filter on the garage shelf keep it mowing without a trip to the store.
**Pros:** Low price with 3-in-1; high rear wheels; simple design; easy to store. **Cons:** Push only; steel deck needs care.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Troy-Bilt+TB110&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Cut for a Push Mower: Cub Cadet SC 100 21-Inch

blocks.p: The SC 100 costs more than entry push mowers and earns the difference with cut quality and a sturdier feel. The deck is contoured to stand grass up before the blade hits it, and owners often say the lawn looks neater afterward than with entry-level push mowers. An adjustable, well-padded handle and a deck that bags, mulches or side-discharges round out the package. It weighs more than the most basic models, which some owners say makes it feel more planted, and Cub Cadet's dealer network helps when it needs service. On a small, flat lawn the Craftsman or Troy-Bilt does the job for less, so buy the SC 100 when the finish matters to you and you want a push mower that feels more solid.
**Pros:** Clean, even cut; comfortable handle; solid feel; dealer support. **Cons:** Costs more than entry push mowers; heavier than basic models.

sections.h: Is a Gas Mower Still Worth It Over Battery?

blocks.p: For some lawns, yes. On a lawn under about a quarter acre that gets cut on schedule, a current battery mower starts with a button, stays quiet and needs almost no upkeep. Gas still wins in three situations.

blocks.h3: Where does gas win?

blocks.p: Large lawns, where one tank keeps going when a battery mower would need a second pack. Thick, tall or wet grass, where a gas engine holds blade speed while battery runtime drops steeply. And irregular mowing, where the grass often gets ahead of you and you need steady power to catch up.

blocks.h3: How do the costs compare?

blocks.p: A basic gas push mower often undercuts a similar battery kit at purchase. Over time, gas needs oil, plugs, filters and stabilizer every season, while a battery mower may eventually need a replacement pack. If you already own batteries from one tool platform, that tips a small lawn toward battery.

blocks.h3: What about the best gas engine for mowing a home lawn?

blocks.p: Most walk-behinds use single-cylinder overhead-valve engines from Briggs and Stratton, Kohler or the mower brand's own line. For a home lawn, engine reliability depends far more on fresh fuel and clean filters than on the badge, so choose a mower with good local parts support.

sections.h: Should You Get a Gas Push Mower or a Self-Propelled One?

blocks.p: Small and level means push; bigger than roughly a quarter acre, or any real grade, means self-propelled.

blocks.h3: Why choose push?

blocks.p: No drive means less weight, a lower price and fewer parts to wear. On a small level lawn, the best gas push mower is usually the simplest one.

blocks.h3: Front or rear-wheel drive?

blocks.p: Front drive is cheaper and turns easily but loses grip uphill and as the bag fills. Rear drive holds traction on slopes and while bagging. Our [self-propelled mower guide](/best-self-propelled-lawn-mower/) compares drive layouts, including battery options, in more depth.

blocks.h3: Who will be mowing?

blocks.p: A lighter push mower is easier for some people to steer and store, while a powered drive helps anyone who finds shoving a heavy machine tiring. Check handle height and controls in person before you buy.

sections.h: What Engine Size and Deck Should a Gas Mower Have?

blocks.p: For a 21-inch walk-behind, an engine in the common 140 to 190 cc range is plenty, and a 21-inch deck suits most yards. More displacement helps in dense grass and on self-propelled models, where the engine also drives the wheels.

blocks.h3: What is the highest cc a homeowner needs?

blocks.p: The top of that range is enough for a 21 or 22-inch deck in thick grass. Chasing a bigger number adds weight and fuel use without improving the cut, which depends on blade speed and deck shape.

blocks.h3: Are easy-start features worth it?

blocks.p: Automatic chokes let many modern mowers start on one pull, and some add electric start. Reliable starting still depends mostly on fresh fuel and clean filters, so a large premium for start features alone is hard to justify.

blocks.h3: Steel or cast aluminum deck?

blocks.p: Stamped steel decks are common and affordable but rust over time, especially at seams, when wet clippings stay packed inside. Cast aluminum decks, like the Toro Super Recycler's, do not rust and often outlive the engine.

blocks.h3: What else matters on the deck?

blocks.p: A mulching deck shape that keeps clippings airborne, a washout port for a garden hose, single-point height adjustment, larger rear wheels for rough ground and ball-bearing wheels that outlast plain bushings. If garage space is tight, look for an engine designed to stand on end for storage without leaking oil into the air filter.

sections.h: What Gas Should You Use, and How Do You Maintain a Gas Mower?

blocks.p: Use fresh gasoline with no more than 10 percent ethanol unless the manual allows more, and keep up a simple seasonal routine of oil, plug, filter and blade.

blocks.h3: Why does old fuel cause problems?

blocks.p: Gas begins degrading within weeks, and ethanol blends absorb moisture and leave varnish in the carburetor. Buy only what you will burn in about a month, store it in an approved can somewhere cool and add stabilizer if it will sit longer. Ethanol-free or canned small-engine fuel costs more but can prevent a carburetor cleaning.

blocks.h3: How often should you change the oil?

blocks.p: Most makers call for the first change after break-in, often within the first five hours, then at least once a season or every 50 hours. Check the dipstick before each mow, since walk-behinds hold only a small amount. Use the viscosity in the manual, often SAE 30 for warm weather or 10W-30 where temperatures swing.

blocks.h3: When should you replace the spark plug and air filter?

blocks.p: Replace the plug every season or on the manual's schedule, and check the air filter often in dry, dusty weather. Paper filters get replaced; many foam filters can be washed and re-oiled.

blocks.h3: How often should you sharpen the blade?

blocks.p: At least once a season, more often on large lawns, sandy soil or after hitting debris. Disconnect the spark plug wire first, block the blade, keep the original angle and balance it before reinstalling. A spare blade makes the swap quick.

blocks.h3: Which gas lawn mowers are the most low-maintenance?

blocks.p: Simple push mowers with no drive system have the fewest parts to service, and cast aluminum decks remove rust from the list. Whatever you own, this routine takes about twenty minutes a season.

sections.h: Why Won't a Gas Lawn Mower Start, and How Do You Winterize It?

blocks.p: Usually because of old fuel, then a fouled spark plug, a clogged air filter or a gummed carburetor, roughly in that order. Work through them cheapest first.

blocks.h3: What should you check first?

blocks.p: The fuel. Anything older than about a month is suspect, and gas that smells sour or looks darker than fresh fuel should be drained. Next, pull the plug: replace it if it is wet, black or fouled, and make sure the wire is firmly attached. Then check the air filter and, on mowers with a primer bulb, press it the number of times the manual says and look for cracks.

blocks.h3: When is it the carburetor?

blocks.p: If the engine still will not fire after a winter with fuel in the tank, the carburetor likely needs cleaning. Small-engine shops do this routinely, and on many budget mowers an aftermarket carburetor is inexpensive. Also confirm the blade brake engages and releases properly, since a faulty brake cable can stop the engine from turning over.

blocks.h3: How do you winterize a gas mower?

blocks.p: Run the tank dry, or fill it with stabilized fresh gas and idle a few minutes so treated fuel reaches the carburetor. Change the oil, clean under the deck, sharpen the blade and store the mower somewhere dry, away from furnaces, water heaters and other ignition sources. Take any electric-start battery indoors.

blocks.h3: How do you use a gas mower safely?

blocks.p: Refuel outdoors with the engine off and cool, never run it in a closed garage or shed because of carbon monoxide, clear the lawn of sticks and toys first, and wear sturdy shoes plus eye and ear protection. On slopes, mow across the face rather than up and down.

sections.h: Are Gas Lawn Mowers Being Banned, and How Much Do They Cost?

blocks.p: Not nationwide. California has moved to phase out sales of most new small off-road gas engines, including lawn mowers, so shoppers there will find few or no new gas walk-behinds in stores. Every gas mower sold in the US must meet EPA emissions standards, and some cities and homeowners associations limit noise or the hours gas equipment can run.

blocks.h3: What happened to Honda mowers?

blocks.p: Honda has wound down production of residential walk-behind mowers for the US market, and remaining HRX and HRR models are mostly dealer stock. Parts support should continue, so a well-priced leftover is still worth considering, but it is no longer a line to plan around. If you are replacing an older Lawn-Boy or Honda walk-behind, any self-propelled pick here with a 21 or 22-inch deck is a like-for-like swap.

blocks.h3: How much does a gas lawn mower cost to buy and run?

blocks.p: Retail pricing runs in tiers: entry push mowers at the low end, self-propelled models in the middle and premium aluminum-deck machines at the top, often two to three times the price of a basic push mower. Do-it-yourself upkeep for oil, a plug, a filter and stabilizer typically runs a few tens of dollars a year. A better-built mower that gets good care often costs less per year than a cheap one replaced every few seasons.

blocks.h3: What else should you budget for?

blocks.p: A spare blade, a fuel can and stabilizer, and a string trimmer for edges. Our [weed eater picks](/best-weed-eater/) cover the trimmers that finish what a walk-behind cannot reach.

mistakes: Leaving fuel in the tank over winter

Old gas is the number one reason a mower refuses to fire in spring. At season's end, run the tank dry or fill it with stabilized fresh gas and let the engine run until treated fuel reaches the carburetor. During the season, buy fuel in small batches you will use within about a month.
Buying a push mower for a sloped or large lawn

Muscling a push mower over hills or a large lawn each week gets old quickly. Once you pass about a quarter acre or face a real grade, spend the extra on a powered drive, and make it rear-wheel if the yard climbs.

Small engines live on clean oil. Glance at the dipstick every time you mow and drain the oil each season or at 50 hours, whichever arrives first. Running low or on dirty oil shortens engine life and can cause sudden failure, so keep a spare quart on the shelf.

A dull blade tears grass instead of cutting it, and the ragged tips turn brown within a day and invite disease. Sharpen at least once a season, balance the blade after sharpening, and replace it when it is bent, cracked or worn thin.
Running the mower in an enclosed space

Gas engines produce carbon monoxide, which builds quickly in a closed garage or shed and has no smell. Start and run the mower outdoors only, keep the engine outside while it runs, and let it cool before you wheel it back in.
bottomLine: Gas is the right call for big lawns, dense or frequently overgrown grass, and owners who never want to watch a charge meter. Push models cover small flat yards; bigger or hillier lawns need a powered drive, ideally on the rear wheels. The Toro Super Recycler and Recycler 22 are the best gas lawn mowers for most yards, and the Craftsman M115 and Troy-Bilt TB110 cover the tightest budgets. Fresh fuel, a seasonal oil change, a new plug and filter, a sharp blade and careful winter storage keep any of them starting on the first or second pull.

faqs.q: What is the best gas lawn mower?
faqs.a: The Toro 21-Inch Super Recycler Personal Pace is the best gas lawn mower for most buyers because its cast aluminum deck cannot rust and its Personal Pace drive matches your walking speed. The Toro Recycler 22-Inch offers most of that ease for less, and the Craftsman M115 is the best low-cost push option.

faqs.q: What is the best gas push mower on the market?
faqs.a: For small, flat lawns, the Craftsman M115 and Troy-Bilt TB110 are the best gas push mowers on a budget, both with 21-inch 3-in-1 decks. The Cub Cadet SC 100 costs more but leaves a cleaner cut and feels sturdier. All three suit lawns under about a quarter acre without slopes.

faqs.q: Which gas lawn mower is good for a typical suburban lawn?
faqs.a: On a quarter to half acre, the Toro Recycler 22-Inch Personal Pace gives the best value, pairing an easy drive with a deck that mulches well. If you want a machine that lasts a decade, spend more on the rust-proof Super Recycler. Small flat lawns are fine with a push mower.

faqs.q: Is a gas mower better than a battery mower?
faqs.a: Gas is better for large lawns, thick or wet grass and irregular mowing, where runtime and steady power matter. Battery is better for small to mid-size lawns cut on schedule, because it is quieter and needs almost no maintenance. Owning batteries from one tool platform tips a smaller lawn toward battery.

faqs.q: How often should you change the oil in a gas lawn mower?
faqs.a: Change it after the first few hours of break-in, then at least once a season or about every 50 hours, which is what most manufacturers specify. Check the dipstick before each mow, use the oil type in the manual, and drain it warm so it flows out quickly and carries more contaminants.

faqs.q: Why won't my gas lawn mower start?
faqs.a: Old fuel is the most common cause, followed by a fouled spark plug, a clogged air filter and a gummed-up carburetor. Drain fuel older than about a month, replace the plug, swap or clean the filter and check the primer bulb. If it still will not start, the carburetor likely needs cleaning.

faqs.q: Are Honda gas mowers still available?
faqs.a: Mostly as leftover stock. Honda stopped building homeowner walk-behinds for the US, so the HRX and HRR units you still see are mostly leftover dealer stock. They are still good mowers and parts should remain available, but do not count on finding one new for much longer.
